papers.title: Concept Bottleneck Models
papers.venue: ICML (PMLR v119), Koh, Nguyen, Tang, Mussmann, Pierson, Kim, Liang
papers.relevance: The origin. Defines independent / sequential / joint training and the soft-vs-hard concept distinction that the whole leakage literature is built on. Already shows joint training trades concept fidelity for task accuracy.
papers.implication: Any model claiming 'utility is composed from perceived outcomes' must state which of the three training regimes it uses, and report the hard/discretised variant. A jointly-trained soft bottleneck is the known-leaky configuration; presenting only that configuration reads as a 2020-era baseline.

papers.title: On Completeness-aware Concept-Based Explanations in Deep Neural Networks
papers.venue: NeurIPS (Yeh, Kim, Arik, Li, Pfister, Ravikumar)
papers.relevance: Introduces the completeness score: how sufficient a concept set is for reproducing model behaviour, formalised as concepts being a sufficient statistic of the prediction. Also ConceptSHAP for per-concept importance.
papers.implication: Demands a sufficiency statement: if perceived outcomes mediate utility, then Y should be conditionally independent of the raw attributes given the outcome representation. A completeness/sufficiency number is the minimum quantitative evidence for a mediation claim; without it 'mediated' is a diagram, not a result.

papers.title: Concept whitening for interpretable image recognition
papers.relevance: Decorrelates and normalises the latent space so axes align with named concepts. The canonical orthogonality/decorrelation fix, predating the leakage papers.
papers.implication: Axis-wise or orthogonality constraints on a concept layer are a 2020 technique. A 2026 paper cannot present 'each outcome head gets its own axis' as an architectural contribution; it is the expected default.

papers.title: Do Concept Bottleneck Models Learn as Intended?
papers.venue: arXiv:2105.04289; ICLR 2021 workshop (Margeloiu, Ashman, Bhatt, Chen, Jamnik, Weller)
papers.relevance: Uses post-hoc saliency to show CBM concept predictors attend to input regions unrelated to the concept: the concepts 'do not correspond to anything semantically meaningful in input space'.
papers.implication: Establishes that a concept predictor scoring well on concept accuracy is not evidence the concept is what the model encodes. Demands an input-attribution or ablation check that each outcome head reads the part of the input it claims to read.

papers.title: Promises and Pitfalls of Black-Box Concept Learning Models
papers.relevance: The canonical leakage diagnosis. Soft concept representations encode information beyond the predefined concepts; leakage persists even when the concepts are fully independent in the data; natural mitigations (e.g. sigmoid squashing, independent training) do not fully remove it. Explains the mechanism.
papers.implication: This is the paper a reviewer means by 'semantic expansion rather than perceived outcomes'. It demands the synthetic-control experiment: construct data where the perceived-outcome channel is known to carry nothing beyond the attributes, and show the model's outcome channel then receives no weight. If it still gets weight, the channel is leaking the attributes back.

papers.title: Addressing Leakage in Concept Bottleneck Models
papers.relevance: Diagnoses the soft-vs-hard performance gap as two separate causes: violation of the Markov assumption C -> Y (measured by a proposed completeness score) and inflexibility of the concept predictor. Fixes: an explicit side-channel model for the residual, and an autoregressive concept predictor.
papers.implication: The single most demanding reference here. It establishes (a) the completeness score as the standard test of whether concepts are sufficient, and (b) the side-channel as the legitimate, declared place for information the concepts do not carry. A paper whose gains come from an 'amplified observed-attribute channel' is running Havasi's side-channel without labelling it as one; the required report is task accuracy with the side-channel ablated to zero.

papers.title: GlanceNets: Interpretable, Leak-proof Concept-based Models
papers.relevance: Defines interpretability as alignment between the learned representation and the data-generating process, and achieves leak-proofing via disentangled representation learning plus open-set recognition.
papers.implication: Sets the bar that 'interpretable' means identifiable with respect to a generative process, not merely 'has names attached'. A perceived-outcome model must say what generative process its outcomes are aligned to and how alignment is tested, or concede the names are labels of convenience.

papers.title: Concept Embedding Models: Beyond the Accuracy-Explainability Trade-Off
papers.venue: NeurIPS 35 (Espinosa Zarlenga, Barbiero, Ciravegna, Marra, Giannini, Diligenti, Shams, Precioso, Melacci, Weller, Lio, Jamnik)
papers.relevance: Replaces scalar concept activations with per-concept positive/negative embeddings, recovering black-box accuracy while keeping interventions effective. The dominant architecture for CBMs with incomplete concept supervision.
papers.implication: CEM is the required baseline for any 'we needed extra capacity per concept' argument. A multi-dimensional per-outcome representation is CEM, 2022. It also makes the harder point: CEM buys accuracy precisely by carrying side information inside the concept embedding, so accuracy gains from a richer concept channel are the expected leakage signature, not evidence of content.

papers.title: Towards learning to explain with concept bottleneck models: mitigating information leakage
papers.venue: arXiv:2211.03656; ICLR 2022 Workshop on Socially Responsible ML (Lockhart, Marchesotti, Magazzeni, Veloso)
papers.relevance: Monte-Carlo dropout on the concept predictor as a leakage mitigation for soft concept labels.
papers.implication: Minor, but closes off 'we add stochasticity to the concept layer to stop leakage' as a novel move.

papers.title: Post-hoc Concept Bottleneck Models
papers.relevance: Turns any network into a CBM post hoc, and introduces PCBM-h, the hybrid that fits the residual with the original embedding when the concept bank is not expressive enough. On CIFAR-100 the concepts alone fail and the residual channel recovers all the accuracy.
papers.implication: This is the precedent that makes the reviewer's third concern lethal. The field already knows that a residual/observed-feature channel can supply essentially all of the accuracy while the concept layer supplies the story. The demanded table is: concepts-only, residual-only, and both — with the concepts-only number reported as the interpretable model's real accuracy.

papers.title: Label-free Concept Bottleneck Models
papers.relevance: GPT-3 generates the concept set; CLIP-Dissect projects features into it; no concept labels needed.
papers.implication: LLM-generated concept vocabularies are settled prior art from 2023. 'We use an LLM to produce the intermediate semantic layer' is not a methodological contribution in 2026.

papers.title: Language in a Bottle: Language Model Guided Concept Bottlenecks for Interpretable Image Classification
papers.venue: CVPR 2023 (Yang, Panagopoulou, Zhou, Jin, Callison-Burch, Yatskar)
papers.relevance: GPT-3 writes sentential concepts, CLIP aligns them to inputs, a submodular objective selects a discriminative and diverse bottleneck. Beats linear probes in the few-shot regime and matches them with more data.
papers.implication: LaBo is the direct ancestor of 'LLM writes sentences, frozen encoder embeds them, small model reads them'. It also pins down where such systems genuinely help — data-scarce regimes — which is the honest framing for a narrative channel, rather than 'the text carries perceived outcomes'.

papers.title: Learning Concise and Descriptive Attributes for Visual Recognition
papers.relevance: Across 8 datasets, LLM-generated attributes in large quantity perform almost the same as random words. Motivates a learning-to-search method that gets comparable accuracy with 32 attributes instead of 10k.
papers.implication: The decisive control for the 'are the narratives real content or semantic expansion?' question. If random or content-free text at the same dimensionality and the same fitted mixture weight matches the generated narratives, the narratives are a capacity channel. This control is standard since 2023; omitting it is now a reviewable defect, not a nicety.

papers.title: Auxiliary Losses for Learning Generalizable Concept-based Models (coop-CBM)
papers.relevance: Adds an auxiliary task loss plus a concept orthogonal loss (COL) that separates concept representations and tightens intra-concept distance; evaluated under distribution shift on CUB, AwA2, CelebA, TIL.
papers.implication: Orthogonality regularisation between concept representations is standard by 2023. It also sets the evaluation expectation: concept-based claims are tested under distribution shift, not only on an i.i.d. split.

papers.title: Not All Neuro-Symbolic Concepts Are Created Equal: Analysis and Mitigation of Reasoning Shortcuts
papers.relevance: Characterises reasoning shortcuts as unintended optima of the learning objective and gives four conditions under which a model attains high task accuracy with concepts that carry unintended semantics.
papers.implication: Gives the theoretical reason a mediation claim cannot be supported by fit alone: the intended and the shortcut solution are both optima. Demands either extra supervision on the mediator, a structural constraint, or a test that distinguishes the two optima.

papers.title: Do Concept Bottleneck Models Respect Localities?
papers.venue: TMLR 2024 (Raman, Espinosa Zarlenga, Heo, Jamnik); arXiv:2401.01259
papers.relevance: Defines locality — does a concept predictor use the features actually relevant to that concept — and gives three perturbation-based metrics. Finds many deployed concept models fail, because concept predictors cannot cleanly separate distinct concepts.
papers.implication: A directly transferable protocol for tabular/behavioural settings: perturb the attributes that should and should not affect a given perceived outcome, and check the outcome head moves only for the former. Cheap to run and currently absent from most LLM-feature papers.

papers.title: VLG-CBM: Training Concept Bottleneck Models with Vision-Language Guidance
papers.relevance: States and analyses the problem directly: 'even a set of random concepts could achieve comparable test accuracy to state-of-the-art CBMs'. Introduces NEC (Number of Effective Concepts) and ANEC — accuracy measured at a fixed decision-layer sparsity — so that CBMs are compared at equal leakage budget.
papers.implication: Establishes that accuracy comparisons between concept models are meaningless unless the capacity of the layer downstream of the concepts is matched. Any claim that the outcome channel contributes must be made at matched effective capacity, not at matched nominal architecture.

papers.title: Stochastic Concept Bottleneck Models
papers.relevance: Models concept dependencies with an explicit multivariate-normal parameterisation so a single intervention propagates to correlated concepts; a cheaper alternative to Havasi's autoregressive predictor.
papers.implication: Forecloses 'our outcomes are correlated so we model them jointly' as novelty. Also raises the bar on interventions: correlated concepts must be intervened on jointly for the intervention curve to mean anything.

papers.title: Eliminating Information Leakage in Hard Concept Bottleneck Models with Supervised, Hierarchical Concept Learning (SupCBM)
papers.relevance: Attacks leakage in the hard-concept setting via label supervision during concept prediction plus a hierarchical concept construction and an intervention matrix.
papers.implication: Shows that even hard bottlenecks leak when classes are separated by concept configurations that are not genuinely distinct. Relevant if the paper argues discretising the outcome channel settles the question — it does not on its own.

papers.title: Tree-Based Leakage Inspection and Control in Concept Bottleneck Models
papers.venue: arXiv:2410.06352 (Ragkousis, Parbhoo); submitted to and withdrawn from ICLR 2025
papers.relevance: Uses decision trees over the concept layer to localise and control leakage in joint and sequential CBMs, giving per-concept leakage attribution rather than a single scalar.
papers.implication: Usable off the shelf on a low-dimensional utility model: fit a tree from the concept/outcome activations to the residual of the attribute-only model and read off which outcome heads are carrying attribute information. Cite it as an existing tool, not as an idea to reinvent.

papers.title: Leakage and Interpretability in Concept-Based Models
papers.venue: arXiv:2504.14094 (Parisini, Chakraborti, Harbron, MacArthur, Banerji); v2 March 2026
papers.relevance: Information-theoretic framework with two measures: Concepts-Task Leakage (CTL) and Interconcept Leakage (ICL). Shown to predict behaviour under intervention better than existing alternatives; identifies an 'alignment leakage' mode specific to Concept Embedding Models.
papers.implication: The current reference metric pair. A 2026 paper that reports leakage with a bespoke ad-hoc statistic instead of CTL/ICL (or SIS, or NEC) will be asked why. These are the numbers that would settle whether the perceived-outcome layer carries anything beyond the attributes.

papers.title: If Concept Bottlenecks are the Question, are Foundation Models the Answer?
papers.venue: arXiv:2504.19774 (Debole, Barbiero, Giannini, Passerini, Teso, Marconato)
papers.relevance: Empirically compares VLM-supervised concepts against expert annotations and finds VLM supervision can differ sharply from expert labels, and that concept accuracy and concept quality are not strongly correlated.
papers.implication: Directly targets the 'do the narratives capture perceived outcomes?' concern for the foundation-model case. Its lesson: a model-generated semantic layer that scores well on any automatic concept metric is not thereby a faithful one. It demands a human validation of a sample of generated narratives against what the annotator judges the decision-maker actually perceives.

papers.title: A Comprehensive Survey on the Risks and Limitations of Concept-based Models
papers.relevance: Taxonomy of failure modes across supervised and unsupervised concept models: structural issues, training-procedure limitations, problematic assumptions, adversarial vulnerability; concept leakage, entangled representations, limited perturbation robustness, and doubts about whether human interventions actually help.
papers.implication: A survey exists. 'We observe that concept layers can leak' is no longer a finding to report; it is background to cite. Useful for positioning the paper's contribution above the level of re-identifying a known problem.

papers.title: Towards Reasonable Concept Bottleneck Models (CREAM)
papers.venue: arXiv:2506.05014 (Kalampalikis, Gupta, Vitanov, Valera); v2 April 2026
papers.relevance: Lets practitioners encode prior beliefs about concept-concept and concept-task relations (mutual exclusivity, hierarchy, correlation, sparse concept-to-task links) so that only intended information flows are possible — leakage mitigated by design, without hard concepts or extra regularisation. Adds an optional regularised side-channel and a C-to-Y-agnostic interpretability metric for partial side-channel reliance.
papers.implication: The closest existing work to 'a structured, interpretable composition of concepts into an outcome'. Any structural claim about how perceived outcomes compose into utility will be compared to CREAM. Its side-channel metric is also the natural way to quantify how much of the prediction rests on the amplified attribute channel.

papers.title: Bayesian Concept Bottleneck Models with LLM Priors (BC-LLM)
papers.relevance: Iteratively searches an unbounded concept space in a Bayesian framework with the LLM as both concept proposer and prior, with validity guarantees despite LLM miscalibration. Evaluated on image, text and tabular data against interpretable and black-box baselines, with better OOD robustness.
papers.implication: The strongest current LLM-concept baseline, and it covers tabular data — so it is a legitimate comparator for a choice-modelling paper, not merely a vision method. It also sets the standard for rigour: the LLM's proposals are treated as a prior to be corrected by data, not as ground-truth features to be trusted.

papers.title: Quantifying the Accuracy-Interpretability Trade-Off in Concept-Based Sidechannel Models
papers.relevance: Names the family 'Concept Sidechannel Models', introduces the Sidechannel Independence Score (SIS) — contrasting predictions with and without sidechannel information — and SIS regularisation. Finds that state-of-the-art CSMs trained purely for accuracy have low representation interpretability, and that SIS regularisation improves interpretability, intervenability and the quality of the learned interpretable predictor.
papers.implication: This is the paper that turns the reviewer's third concern into a number. A model whose gains rest on an amplified observed-attribute channel is a CSM with high sidechannel reliance; SIS measures exactly that, and SIS regularisation is the off-the-shelf fix. The paper should report SIS (or equivalently the with/without-sidechannel prediction contrast) rather than argue qualitatively about channel attribution.

papers.title: There Was Never a Bottleneck in Concept Bottleneck Models (MCBM)
papers.relevance: Argues CBMs never impose a real bottleneck: the fact that a component predicts a concept does not mean it encodes only that concept. Proposes Minimal CBMs, adding a variational Information Bottleneck term so each representation component retains only information relevant to its own concept.
papers.implication: The sharpest statement of the standard the field now applies. Naming a head after a perceived outcome, and showing it predicts that outcome, proves nothing about what it encodes. Minimality (an upper bound on I(X;C_j) per component) is the current criterion, and it is published — so a 2026 paper cannot propose it.

papers.title: Concepts' Information Bottleneck Models
papers.relevance: An Information Bottleneck regulariser on the concept layer penalising I(X;C) while preserving I(C;Y), yielding minimal-sufficient concept representations; two practical estimators, tested across CBM architectures and datasets; consistently improves accuracy and intervention reliability over vanilla counterparts.
papers.implication: Independent confirmation, at the same venue and year, that IB-regularised concept layers are now the default remedy. Together with MCBM this closes the door on 'we add a mutual-information penalty to keep the concept channel clean' as a 2026 contribution.

papers.title: Rethinking Concept Bottleneck Models: From Pitfalls to Solutions (CBM-Suite)
papers.venue: CVPR 2026 (Tapli, Bouniot, Stammer, Akata, Akbas); arXiv:2603.05629
papers.relevance: Four pitfalls: no pre-evaluation metric for whether a concept set suits a dataset; the linearity problem, where recent CBMs circumvent the bottleneck entirely; the accuracy gap to opaque networks; and thin systematic analysis of backbone/VLM choices. Offers an entropy-based metric for the intrinsic suitability of a concept set, a non-linear layer that preserves concept relevance, and a distillation loss.
papers.implication: The entropy-based suitability metric is the answer to 'is this concept vocabulary even appropriate for this dataset?' — directly usable to ask whether a generated set of perceived outcomes is suited to a given choice dataset before any model is fitted. It also warns that the 'linearity problem' critique (the predictor routes around the bottleneck) is now a named, CVPR-published objection.

papers.title: In Defense of Information Leakage in Concept-based Models
papers.relevance: A position paper by the CEM author, arguing the evidence that leakage harms interpretability is not conclusive; that where concept sets are necessarily incomplete some leakage is required for accurate and intervenable models; and introducing 'benign leakage', which a reframed training objective can deliberately exploit without sacrificing accuracy or intervenability.
papers.implication: The most useful single citation for a rebuttal. It legitimises a model in which the observed-attribute channel carries real weight — but only on the condition that the leakage is declared, characterised as benign under an explicit criterion, and shown not to destroy intervenability. It converts 'the gains come from the attribute channel' from a fatal admission into a design position, provided the paper does the measurement.

papers.title: Measuring What Matters: Synthetic Benchmarks for Concept Bottleneck Models
papers.relevance: Synthetic data generators with controlled data modality, concept choice, annotation quality and completeness, aimed at decision-support and automation settings, for diagnosing failure modes.
papers.implication: Very recent, so not yet an obligation — but it is the template for the experiment that would settle the reviewer's second concern. A synthetic choice dataset in which perceived outcomes are generated separately from observed attributes, with a known ground-truth mediation structure, is the one design under which 'utility is composed from perceived outcomes' is a testable claim rather than an interpretive gloss.

papers.title: Shortcuts and Identifiability in Concept-based Models from a Neuro-Symbolic Lens
papers.relevance: Extends reasoning-shortcut theory from neuro-symbolic predictors to concept-based models, deriving theoretical conditions under which both the concepts and the inference layer are identifiable, and showing high accuracy is attainable with low-quality concepts even when the inference layer is fixed in advance.
papers.implication: Supplies the identifiability vocabulary a mediation claim needs. Fixing the utility form in advance (as choice models do) does not by itself identify the mediator; the paper must argue its conditions hold, or state plainly that its concepts are not claimed to be identified.

already_standard: Observing that soft concept activations encode information beyond their named concepts. Mahinpei et al. 2021, plus the mechanism. Background to cite, not a finding to report.

Hard / binarised / discretised concepts as the leakage-resistant configuration, and the soft-vs-hard accuracy gap as the diagnostic for how much leakage there is. Koh et al. ICML 2020, Havasi et al. NeurIPS 2022.

An explicit side-channel or residual channel carrying what the concepts cannot. Havasi et al. NeurIPS 2022 (side-channel model), Yuksekgonul et al. ICLR 2023 (PCBM-h residual fitting), Kalampalikis et al. 2025 (CREAM's regularised side-channel). An 'amplified observed-attribute channel' is this construct; it is prior art, and the field expects it to be declared and measured, not discovered.

Measuring how much of the prediction rests on the side-channel rather than the concepts. Debot et al. 2025 (Sidechannel Independence Score and SIS regularisation), CREAM's C-to-Y-agnostic interpretability metric. The number exists; a qualitative argument about channel attribution will not pass.
Autoregressive or dependency-aware concept predictors so that concepts are modelled jointly rather than independently. Havasi et al. NeurIPS 2022, Vandenhirtz et al. NeurIPS 2024 (SCBM).

Per-concept vector embeddings instead of scalar activations, to buy back accuracy under incomplete concept supervision. Espinosa Zarlenga et al. NeurIPS 2022 (CEM). Also the cautionary case: CEM's accuracy comes partly from side information carried inside the embedding, so accuracy gains from a richer concept channel are the expected leakage signature.
Orthogonality, decorrelation and whitening constraints on the concept layer. Chen, Bei and Rudin, Nature MI 2020 (concept whitening); Sheth and Ebrahimi Kahou, NeurIPS 2023 (concept orthogonal loss).
Disentanglement and generative-process alignment as leak-proofing. Marconato et al. NeurIPS 2022 (GlanceNets).

Information-bottleneck regularisation of the concept layer — penalising I(X;C) subject to preserving I(C;Y), i.e. minimal-sufficient concepts. Published twice at ICLR 2026 (Almudevar et al., MCBM; Galliamov et al., Concepts' IB). Fully closed as a novelty claim.

LLM-generated concept vocabularies, including free-text sentential concepts embedded by a frozen encoder. Oikarinen et al. ICLR 2023 (Label-free CBM), Yang et al. CVPR 2023 (LaBo), Feng et al. NeurIPS 2025 (BC-LLM, which also covers tabular data). 'An LLM writes the intermediate semantic layer' is 2023 prior art.

The random-concept control: showing that random words or random concept sets match LLM-generated concepts. Yan et al. ICCV 2023 ('LLM-generated attributes in a large quantity perform almost the same as random words'), Srivastava, Yan and Weng, NeurIPS 2024 ('even a set of random concepts could achieve comparable test accuracy'). Running this control is now expected; omitting it is a reviewable defect.
Controlling the capacity of the layer downstream of the concepts so that comparisons are made at equal leakage budget. Srivastava et al. NeurIPS 2024 (NEC / ANEC), extended to NCC at ICLR 2026.

Test-time concept intervention curves as the faithfulness test, and the finding that intervention effectiveness is what distinguishes a real bottleneck from a leaky one. Koh et al. ICML 2020 onwards; central to Havasi et al. 2022, CEM 2022, SCBM 2024.
Completeness / sufficiency scores for a concept set. Yeh et al. NeurIPS 2020; Havasi et al. NeurIPS 2022's completeness score.
Information-theoretic leakage metrics. Parisini et al. 2025 (Concepts-Task Leakage and Interconcept Leakage), Ragkousis and Parbhoo 2024 (tree-based per-concept leakage attribution).
Locality / perturbation tests that a concept predictor uses the input features relevant to that concept. Raman et al., TMLR 2024.
The general observation that concept accuracy and concept quality decorrelate under foundation-model supervision. Debole et al. 2025.
Surveying the failure modes of concept-based models. Sinha and Zhang 2025.
genuinely_open: Leakage in non-perceptual domains. Essentially the entire literature is vision (CUB, AwA2, CelebA, CIFAR, skin lesions), where the raw input is high-dimensional and uninterpretable, so a low-dimensional named layer is obviously a bottleneck. In discrete choice the raw features are already low-dimensional and human-readable, so the concept layer is not narrowing anything — it is re-describing. No accepted definition of leakage covers this case, and 'the concepts are a semantic expansion of the features' is the null hypothesis rather than an anomaly. Formalising leakage when the bottleneck is wider than the input is open and is the natural place for a methods contribution.

Whether leakage is harmful at all. Actively contested as of ICML 2026 (Espinosa Zarlenga, 'In Defense of Information Leakage'), which argues the evidence that leakage reduces interpretability is not conclusive and that some leakage is necessary when concept sets are incomplete. What separates benign from harmful leakage, and how to certify it, is open — and is a defensible position to adopt rather than a weakness to hide.

Leakage measurement for continuous, free-text concept channels. CTL/ICL, SIS, NEC/NCC and the tree-based inspection all assume a finite set of named scalar concepts with known semantics. None of them applies directly to a channel of sentence embeddings, where there is no per-concept activation to inspect. Defining the analogue for a narrative channel is unsolved.

Faithfulness of generated narratives. There is no accepted test that an LLM-written description reports what a decision-maker perceives rather than paraphrasing the tabulated attributes. Debole et al. 2025 shows automatic concept metrics do not track quality; nobody has replaced them for free-text concepts. The available substitutes are human validation on a sample, and a generation ablation in which the narrative generator is denied the attributes it is suspected of paraphrasing.

Intervention semantics for narrative concepts. The field's sharpest faithfulness test is intervening on a concept and watching the prediction move. It is undefined how to set a perceived-outcome narrative to a counterfactual value. Constructing a well-posed intervention over generated text — and showing the utility model responds as the claimed composition predicts — has no established protocol, and would be a genuine contribution.

Empirical identification of mediation. Reasoning-shortcut theory (Marconato et al. NeurIPS 2023; the NeurIPS 2025 concept-based extension) gives conditions under which concepts and inference layer are identifiable, but no practical test for the non-neurosymbolic case, and fixing the inference layer in advance (as a utility form does) is explicitly shown not to suffice. Whether a fixed, parametric, economically-motivated utility form plus a generated mediator can be identified is not answered by existing work.

Ground-truth benchmarks with a known generative concept structure. Only arriving now (Skirzynski et al., June 2026, synthetic CBM benchmarks) and vision/tabular-classification shaped. There is no choice-modelling benchmark where perceived outcomes are generated separately from observed attributes with a known mediation structure. Building one is the single experiment that would convert 'utility is composed from perceived outcomes' into a falsifiable claim, and nobody has built it.

The economics side is empty. There is LLM-assisted choice-model specification (Can LLMs assist choice modelling?, arXiv:2507.21790), LLMs simulating respondents, and LLM feature generation for interpretable ML (Machine Learning journal, 2025) — but no discrete-choice analogue of the CBM leakage literature, no leakage metric for a utility function, and no protocol for showing a semantic layer adds to a mode-choice or purchase model beyond its attributes. Importing the CBM leakage apparatus into random-utility modelling is unclaimed territory.
v2:aa211b4aa02db9b1206726e7b2d94b85ba9b3.verdict: The reviewer's three technical objections are not idiosyncratic — each is the exact standard the concept-bottleneck field settled on between 2021 and 2026, and each has a named metric attached. "Are the narratives perceived outcomes or semantic expansion?" is Mahinpei et al. 2021, and the answer is given by the random-concept control from Yan et al. ICCV 2023 and Srivastava et al. NeurIPS 2024, both of which found LLM concepts match random words. "The gains depend on the amplified observed-attribute channel" is the side-channel problem: Havasi NeurIPS 2022 named it, PCBM-h ICLR 2023 showed the residual channel can supply nearly all the accuracy, and Debot et al. 2025 gives the Sidechannel Independence Score that measures it. "Methodological novelty is limited" is correct as stated: LLM-generated concepts (2023), personalised/embedded concept representations (CEM 2022), orthogonality (2020), information-bottleneck regularisation (ICLR 2026, twice), autoregressive and dependency-aware concept layers (2022, 2024), and sparsity-controlled comparison (NEC 2024) are all closed. None of these can be claimed as new in 2026. The paper cannot win by contesting the objections; it can win by meeting them and by relocating the contribution. Two openings are real. First, no leakage framework applies when the bottleneck is wider than the input — every existing metric assumes a high-dimensional uninterpretable input narrowed to a few named scalars, which is the opposite of a choice model whose attributes are already few and named. That inverted case has no definition of leakage, and defining it is a contribution. Second, there is no intervention semantics for narrative concepts, which is the field's sharpest faithfulness test and the one that has never been ported to free text; a well-posed counterfactual over a generated narrative, with the utility model responding as the claimed composition predicts, would be new. A third, cheaper move is to adopt the ICML 2026 position directly: declare the attribute channel a side-channel, report SIS or the with/without contrast, and argue the leakage is benign under an explicit criterion — which converts the third objection from a fatal admission into a stated design position. The immediate obligations, independent of framing, are: report concepts-only, sidechannel-only and combined accuracies as three separate numbers; run the random/shuffled-text control at matched dimensionality and matched fitted mixture weight; report a completeness or conditional-sufficiency number for the mediation claim; compare at matched effective downstream capacity, not matched nominal architecture; and include BC-LLM (NeurIPS 2025) as the LLM-concept baseline, since it is the one that covers tabular data. The existing uniform-floor control in the repository's audit paper is stronger than the three controls the field normally runs and is worth foregrounding as a methodological contribution in its own right — it is the one control in this space that bounds what mixing anything into a sharp model can buy, and it has no counterpart in the CBM literature.

v2:eb94e5d0024407351a083e5730507b805cbda.key: The pooling machinery (stacking, out-of-fold weights, linear pools of predictive distributions) is textbook 1992-2018 and cannot be claimed as novel in 2026; the *weight-matched uninformative-channel control* ("uniform-floor control") does NOT exist under any name in forecasting, ensembling or ML-evaluation literature and is a legitimate small nameable contribution — but only as a diagnostic, and it is the weakest null available. The defensible re-angle is: method + a ladder of nulls (uniform floor, refit-weight uniform, marginal/climatology floor, shuffled-narrative, attribute-only-narrative) reported alongside a reliability/resolution decomposition of the log score, which is exactly what answers reviewer concerns 2 and 3.

papers.title: Stacked Generalization
papers.relevance: Wolpert's original stacking: train a meta-learner on out-of-fold predictions of base learners. This is the ancestor of any 'fit a mixture weight on held-out folds' procedure.
papers.implication: Cite it and concede it. Any claim that fitting a combination weight out-of-fold is part of the contribution is dead on arrival. Frame the OM-LEU pooling step as 'standard stacking' in one sentence and move the novelty elsewhere.

papers.title: Super Learner
papers.venue: Statistical Applications in Genetics and Molecular Biology 6(1), Article 25
papers.relevance: van der Laan, Polley & Hubbard. V-fold cross-validated convex weights over a library of learners, with an oracle inequality. The canonical formalisation of out-of-fold weight estimation.
papers.implication: Two uses. (a) It is the citation that makes out-of-fold weighting non-novel. (b) Its standard practice of putting a deliberately null learner (SL.mean / intercept-only GLM) in the library as a benchmark is the closest existing relative of your uniform-floor idea — but the null learner's weight is *refit*, not held fixed, so it is not weight-matched. Say this explicitly; it is how you carve out the delta.

papers.title: Using Stacking to Average Bayesian Predictive Distributions (with Discussion)
papers.relevance: Yao, Vehtari, Simpson & Gelman. Stacking generalised from point predictions to predictive distributions, with the log score as the stacking objective and LOO for the out-of-fold step.
papers.implication: This is the exact template of 'linear pool of predictive distributions with log-score-optimal weights fit out-of-fold'. If your combination step is this, you must cite it and present the step as adopted, not invented.

papers.title: Combining Probability Forecasts
papers.venue: Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series B 72(1):71-91
papers.relevance: Ranjan & Gneiting. Proves that any non-trivial weighted average of two or more distinct *calibrated* probability forecasts is necessarily uncalibrated and underconfident; proposes the beta-transformed linear pool as the fix.
papers.implication: The single most damaging-if-ignored citation for your paper. It establishes that linear pooling systematically changes dispersion, i.e. that pool gains and pool losses are entangled with calibration by construction. Use it as the motivation for the uniform-floor control rather than letting a reviewer use it against you. It also gives you a free extra experiment: does a beta-transformed / recalibrated pool retain the OM-LEU gain?

papers.title: Combining Predictive Distributions
papers.relevance: Gneiting & Ranjan. Systematic study of generalized, spread-adjusted and beta-transformed linear pools from the calibration-and-dispersion perspective; shows the traditional linear pool is overdispersed.
papers.implication: The companion result. Together with Ranjan & Gneiting (2010) it lets you state, with citation, that 'mixture gains under the log score are a priori confounded with dispersion/calibration effects' — which is precisely the premise your control is designed to test.

papers.title: Probability Judgments for Continuous Quantities: Linear Combinations and Calibration
papers.relevance: Hora. Theoretical argument that linearly combining well-calibrated expert distributions can only reduce calibration, but that equally weighted pools of *overconfident* experts can improve it.
papers.implication: Directly names the mechanism you are worried about: a pool helps when the base model is overconfident, for reasons that are pure calibration. If your base discrete-choice model is overconfident (it almost certainly is on sparse Amazon data), this is the prior explanation the reviewer will reach for. Pre-empt it.

papers.title: Optimal Prediction Pools
papers.relevance: Geweke & Amisano. Log-score-optimal linear pools; shows the optimal pool typically puts positive weight on several models even when exactly one model has limiting posterior probability 1.
papers.implication: Establishes that a positive fitted mixture weight on a channel is NOT evidence that the channel is true or informative. This is the cleanest published refutation of the implicit argument 'the weight was large, therefore the narratives matter'. Cite it in the sentence where you justify needing a control at all.

papers.title: Forecast Uncertainty, Disagreement, and the Linear Pool
papers.relevance: Knüppel & Krüger. Framework in terms of means and variances of individual vs combined forecasts; the pool's advantage over its components tracks disagreement among components, not correctness.
papers.implication: Gives you a published, quantitative statement that pool improvement is driven by component disagreement/dispersion. Lets you frame your control as isolating the disagreement-driven part from the information-driven part.

papers.title: Jensen's Inequality and the Success of Linear Prediction Pools
papers.venue: Working paper, University of Konstanz (preliminary draft, 22 May 2012); presented at Deutsche Bundesbank
papers.relevance: Krüger. Shows Jensen's inequality sets a lower bound on the success of linear pools relative to their component models, for the log, quadratic and CRPS scores, holding for every realised value of the predictand.
papers.implication: This is the cleanest statement of 'a linear pool cannot be much worse than its components' — the formal skeleton of your uniform-floor argument. CAUTION: it is an unpublished preliminary draft, not a journal article. Do not cite it as published. Better: state the one-line inequality yourself, log[(1-lam)p(y) + lam q(y)] >= log p(y) + log(1-lam), prove it in a footnote, and cite Geweke & Amisano (2011) and Knüppel & Krüger (2022) for the published framing.

papers.title: Probabilistic Forecasts, Calibration and Sharpness
papers.venue: Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series B 69(2):243-268
papers.relevance: Gneiting, Balabdaoui & Raftery. The 'maximise sharpness subject to calibration' paradigm; the standard vocabulary for separating calibration from concentration of a predictive distribution.
papers.implication: Gives you the vocabulary the reviewer's concern is really about. Reframe reviewer point 3 in these terms in the rebuttal: the question is whether the narrative channel adds sharpness-at-fixed-calibration, or only fixes calibration.

papers.title: Reliability, Sufficiency, and the Decomposition of Proper Scores
papers.venue: Quarterly Journal of the Royal Meteorological Society 135(643):1512-1519
papers.relevance: Bröcker. Generalises Murphy's Brier-score reliability/resolution/uncertainty decomposition to any strictly proper scoring rule and to finite-valued targets.
papers.implication: THE tool for the rebuttal. Report your NLL decomposed into reliability + resolution + uncertainty rather than as a single number. A uniform floor can only improve the reliability term (and it strictly shrinks resolution). If the narrative channel's gain shows up in resolution, reviewer concern 3 is answered with a measurement rather than an argument.

papers.title: Kullback-Leibler Divergence as a Forecast Skill Score with Classic Reliability-Resolution-Uncertainty Decomposition
papers.relevance: Weijs, van Nooijen & van de Giesen. Reformulates the log/ignorance score as a KL divergence and gives the information-theoretic reliability/resolution/uncertainty decomposition for categorical forecasts.
papers.implication: The directly usable version for discrete choice: your outcome IS categorical and your score IS the log score. This is the specific decomposition to implement. It also gives you the right skill-score normalisation (relative to the marginal/climatological forecast) so that your Amazon numbers stop being sensitive to choice-set construction — which answers reviewer concern 4.

papers.title: From Ensemble Forecasts to Predictive Distribution Functions
papers.relevance: Bröcker & Smith. Affine kernel dressing, in which a weight on the *climatological* distribution is fitted jointly with the dressing parameters — an explicit, fitted probability floor inside a predictive mixture.
papers.implication: This is the nearest thing in the literature to a 'floor' component in a pool, and it is nearly 20 years old. It is presented as a *modelling device* (to avoid unbounded log scores), never as a *control*. Cite it to show you know the operation is old, and state that the contribution is the inferential use, not the operation.

papers.title: On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks
papers.venue: Proceedings of the 34th International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 70:1321-1330
papers.relevance: Guo, Pleiss, Sun & Weinberger. Modern networks are badly miscalibrated; single-parameter temperature scaling fixes most of it.
papers.implication: Gives you a mandatory extra baseline: temperature-scale the base choice model alone, on the same out-of-fold data used to fit the mixture weight. If that recovers most of the pooled gain, the narrative channel is adding calibration. Running this and reporting it is far more persuasive than arguing.

papers.title: Designing and Interpreting Probes with Control Tasks
papers.relevance: Hewitt & Liang. Introduces control tasks — a structurally matched but information-free version of the task — and 'selectivity' (task accuracy minus control accuracy) as the quantity to report.
papers.implication: The intellectual template you should explicitly claim descent from. Your uniform-floor control is the predictive-pooling analogue of a control task, and saying so both establishes rigour and honestly bounds the novelty claim. Adopt their reporting convention: report the gap (gain over the matched null), never the raw gain.

papers.title: Information-Theoretic Probing with Minimum Description Length
papers.relevance: Voita & Titov. MDL probing: measure the code length needed to extract the property, which penalises probes that merely memorise; more informative and more stable than accuracy-based probing with control tasks.
papers.implication: The right tool for reviewer concern 2 (do narratives capture perceived outcomes or just re-describe observed features?). Compute the description length of the choice labels given (a) attributes only, (b) attributes + narratives. If narratives are semantic expansion of attributes, online-code length barely drops.

papers.title: Information-Theoretic Probing for Linguistic Structure
papers.relevance: Pimentel, Valvoda, Hall Maudslay, Zmigrod, Williams & Cotterell. Formalises probing as mutual-information estimation and argues you should use the strongest probe available for a tighter bound.
papers.implication: Supplies the framing to say your narrative channel's contribution is a lower bound on I(narrative; choice | attributes), and that the uniform-floor control is what makes the bound non-vacuous. Also warns against the reviewer's likely counter that you used a weak head.

papers.title: Permutation Tests for Studying Classifier Performance
papers.relevance: Ojala & Garriga. Two permutation tests: permute labels to test whether real class structure was found; permute features within classes to test whether feature dependencies are being exploited.
papers.implication: The canonical citation for label-shuffling and feature-shuffling controls, and the reason a reviewer will call such controls standard. Use the *second* test as the model for your shuffled-narrative control: permute narratives across instances *within an observed-attribute stratum*, which preserves the marginal narrative distribution and any generic semantic content while destroying the per-instance match. That is the control that actually separates 'perceived outcome' from 'semantic expansion'.

papers.title: Ranking a Random Feature for Variable and Feature Selection
papers.relevance: Stoppiglia, Dreyfus, Dubois & Oussar. The probe/contrast variable: inject a known-random feature and keep only features that outrank it, with an explicit risk level.
papers.implication: Establishes the random-feature control as 23 years old. Do not present 'we compared against a random channel' as new. Do cite it as the ancestor of the idea and point out that it fixes a *selection threshold*, not a *mixture weight*.

papers.title: Feature Selection with the Boruta Package
papers.relevance: Kursa & Rudnicki. Shadow features: permuted copies of the real features form a noise baseline; a feature is kept only if it beats its shadow.
papers.implication: The most widely used shadow/permuted-copy control in practice. Same point: the substitution logic is standard; only its application to a fitted mixture weight is not.

papers.title: All Models are Wrong, but Many are Useful: Learning a Variable's Importance by Studying an Entire Class of Prediction Models Simultaneously
papers.relevance: Fisher, Rudin & Dominici. Model class reliance; connects single-model permutation importance to conditional variable importance and shows importance is model-dependent, not a property of the data alone.
papers.implication: Arms you against 'your ablation only shows your particular model relied on the channel'. Reporting reliance across a class (e.g. across the amplification hyperparameter, across seeds, across choice-set constructions) is the response to reviewer concern 4 about hyperparameter sensitivity.

papers.title: Deep Ensembles Work, But Are They Necessary?
papers.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 35 (NeurIPS 2022)
papers.relevance: Abe, Buchanan, Pleiss, Zemel & Cunningham. Shows the claimed distinct benefits of deep ensembles (uncertainty quality, robustness) are reproduced by a single larger network, i.e. the ensembling mechanism was not what was doing the work.
papers.implication: The closest ML precedent in spirit for your whole paper's reframing: an accepted top-venue paper whose contribution is a control showing a popular mechanism's gains have a mundane explanation. It is proof that this kind of contribution is publishable at NeurIPS/ICLR — useful for the 'novelty is limited' rebuttal.

papers.title: Are We Really Making Much Progress? A Worrying Analysis of Recent Neural Recommendation Approaches
papers.venue: Proceedings of the 13th ACM Conference on Recommender Systems (RecSys 2019)
papers.relevance: Ferrari Dacrema, Cremonesi & Jannach. Only 7 of 18 neural top-n recommenders were reproducible, and 6 of those 7 were beaten by well-tuned simple baselines. Best Long Paper.
papers.implication: Directly addresses reviewer concern 4 (missing baselines, dataset construction sensitivity, reproducibility). Cite it as the reason you added tuned classical baselines and fixed dataset-construction protocols, and report baseline tuning budgets explicitly.

papers.title: Prediction, Learning, and Games
papers.relevance: Cesa-Bianchi & Lugosi. Prediction with expert advice under logarithmic loss; mixture forecasters and the standard device of mixing with a uniform/prior component to keep the logarithmic loss bounded and regret finite.
papers.implication: The citation establishing that 'mix with uniform so the log loss cannot blow up' is a foundational, decades-old device in online learning — alongside Laplace/add-alpha and Krichevsky-Trofimov estimators in universal coding. Concede the operation is ancient; claim only the inferential reframing.

papers.title: Label-Free Concept Bottleneck Models
papers.relevance: Oikarinen, Das, Nguyen & Weng. Automatically generates the concept set and concept labels with pretrained/language models, removing the manual-annotation requirement of concept bottlenecks.
papers.implication: Reviewer concern 1 in citation form: LLM-generated features feeding an interpretable bottleneck is a 2023 idea. Your novelty cannot be 'LLM concepts + interpretable bottleneck'. It has to be the *outcome-mediated* structure (concepts are latent perceived consequences of a choice, not descriptions of the item) plus the evaluation protocol.

papers.title: Language in a Bottle: Language Model Guided Concept Bottlenecks for Interpretable Image Classification
papers.venue: IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR 2023)
papers.relevance: Yang, Panagopoulou, Zhou, Jin, Callison-Burch & Yatskar. LLM-proposed concepts form the bottleneck, with a linear layer over concept scores giving an interpretable classifier.
papers.implication: Same as above; the two together are the pair a reviewer would cite to say the architecture is not new. Cite both yourself, in a related-work paragraph that states plainly what is shared and what is not, rather than being caught.

already_standard: Out-of-fold / cross-validated estimation of combination weights. Wolpert (1992) for stacking, van der Laan et al. (2007) for the cross-validated convex-weight version with an oracle inequality. Not claimable.

Linear pooling of predictive distributions with log-score-optimal weights. Ranjan & Gneiting (2010), Geweke & Amisano (2011), Yao et al. (2018). Not claimable, and Yao et al. is the template your combination step most closely matches.

The fact that a linear pool beats the weighted average of its components' log scores by Jensen's inequality, and therefore that positive pool gain is not evidence of component correctness. Implied by Geweke & Amisano (2011); stated explicitly in Krüger's 2012 unpublished draft; quantified via disagreement in Knüppel & Krüger (2022). State the one-line inequality with a footnote proof; do not claim it.

The fact that pooling systematically changes calibration and dispersion — a pool of calibrated forecasts is necessarily uncalibrated and underconfident. Ranjan & Gneiting (2010), Gneiting & Ranjan (2013), Hora (2004). This is the published core of the reviewer's concern; it is fully established.

Mixing a predictive distribution with a uniform or climatological distribution to bound the logarithmic loss. Ancient and multiply named: Laplace / add-alpha smoothing, Krichevsky-Trofimov estimators, Jelinek-Mercer interpolation in language modelling, epsilon-contamination, mixture forecasters in Cesa-Bianchi & Lugosi (2006), and a fitted climatology weight in affine kernel dressing (Bröcker & Smith, 2008). The OPERATION is not novel under any framing.

Decomposing a proper score into reliability (calibration), resolution (information) and uncertainty. Murphy's Brier decomposition; generalised to all strictly proper scores by Bröcker (2009) and to the log score / categorical forecasts by Weijs et al. (2010). Available and directly applicable — use it, do not reinvent it.

Skill scores measured against a reference (uniform, marginal, climatological) forecast. Standard meteorological verification practice for decades. Reporting a skill score relative to the marginal choice distribution is expected, not novel.

Permutation / shuffle controls to test whether a channel carries information. Label permutation and within-class feature permutation: Ojala & Garriga (2010). Random-feature (probe/contrast variable) controls: Stoppiglia et al. (2003). Shadow features: Kursa & Rudnicki (2010). Permutation importance and its model-class generalisation: Fisher, Rudin & Dominici (2019).

Matched information-free control conditions for representation-based claims. Control tasks and selectivity: Hewitt & Liang (2019). MDL/information-theoretic probing: Voita & Titov (2020), Pimentel et al. (2020). A reviewer will consider these the standard against which your controls are judged.

Including a deliberately null learner (SL.mean, intercept-only GLM) in an ensemble library as a benchmark. Routine SuperLearner practice. Crucially, its weight is REFIT, so it is not weight-matched — this is the gap your control occupies.

LLM-generated features feeding an interpretable bottleneck. Label-Free CBM (ICLR 2023), LaBo (CVPR 2023), on top of concept bottleneck models (Koh et al., ICML 2020 — verify this citation before using it; I did not confirm it by search). The architecture pattern is three years old.
Reproducibility and baseline-tuning standards for recommendation-style evaluations. Ferrari Dacrema, Cremonesi & Jannach (RecSys 2019). Expected, not a contribution.
genuinely_open: The weight-matched uninformative-channel control itself. I searched forecasting, ensembling, probing, feature-selection and ML-evaluation literature and found NO named device that holds a fitted mixture weight lambda-hat fixed, substitutes the uniform (or marginal) distribution for the added channel, and reports the residual gain as the information claim. The nearest relatives all differ in one specific way: climatology/reference forecasts are baselines outside the mixture; SL.mean is inside the mixture but with a refit weight; Bröcker & Smith's climatology weight is a modelling device not a control; control tasks and shadow features apply the substitution to inputs, not to a mixture component. Naming it (suggested: 'weight-matched uninformative-channel control', or 'calibration-null pool') and positioning it as the predictive-pooling analogue of Hewitt & Liang's control task is defensible and honest. Do not oversell it as a method family; sell it as a diagnostic protocol.

A significance test for 'the channel's gain exceeds its matched uninformative null'. There is no established sampling distribution for this statistic when lambda-hat is itself estimated out-of-fold. A paired bootstrap or Diebold-Mariano-style test over per-observation log-score differences is the natural route, but the nested/degenerate-null case (true channel vs uniform channel at the same weight) has not, as far as I can find, been worked out. Developing even a bootstrap procedure here is a real, small, publishable contribution.

Extending the reliability/resolution/uncertainty decomposition (Bröcker 2009; Weijs et al. 2010) to discrete choice with per-instance variable choice sets. Those decompositions assume a fixed, low-dimensional forecast space and require binning. Amazon-style choice sets vary per instance in size and composition. A workable decomposition for this setting is not in the literature and is exactly what your paper needs.

Whether LLM narratives encode perceived *outcomes* rather than paraphrases of observed attributes. No established test exists. The strongest available design is a ladder: (i) narratives generated from observed attributes only, no user history, no consequence reasoning; (ii) full narratives; (iii) narratives shuffled across instances within an attribute stratum (Ojala & Garriga's within-class permutation). If (ii) beats (i) and (iii), the outcome-mediated part is carrying something. Combine with MDL probing (Voita & Titov 2020) for a code-length version of the same claim. Building this ladder and reporting it is the real answer to reviewer concern 2.

Whether a recalibrated pool (beta-transformed linear pool, Ranjan & Gneiting 2010; spread-adjusted pool, Gneiting & Ranjan 2013) preserves the OM-LEU gain. Nobody has run recalibrated pooling on LLM-feature-augmented choice models. If the gain survives beta-transformation, the calibration explanation is largely ruled out and you have a positive, publishable result rather than a defensive one.

The tension between super-learner theory and the log score. Cross-validated weight-selection oracle inequalities assume bounded loss; the log score is unbounded without a probability floor. So the floor is simultaneously what makes the weight-estimation theory valid AND what confounds the information claim. This tension appears not to be discussed anywhere and is worth a paragraph — it is the theoretical reason the control is needed, not merely an empirical worry.

Attributing mixture gain between the amplified observed-attribute channel and the narrative channel (reviewer concern 3). There is no standard attribution method for a multi-channel pool under the log score. Reporting a full factorial — amplification on/off crossed with narrative real/uniform/shuffled/attribute-only — plus the resolution term of each cell, is the most defensible thing available, and no one has proposed a better one.

The reviewer is right about novelty as the paper is currently framed, and the fix is to move the claim rather than defend it. Every component of the combination machinery is established: stacking (Wolpert 1992), cross-validated convex weights (van der Laan et al. 2007), log-score stacking of predictive distributions (Yao et al. 2018), the result that linear pools are necessarily miscalibrated (Ranjan & Gneiting 2010; Gneiting & Ranjan 2013; Hora 2004), the result that positive pool weight is not evidence of component correctness (Geweke & Amisano 2011; Knüppel & Krüger 2022), and the practice of mixing with uniform/climatology to bound the log loss (Cesa-Bianchi & Lugosi 2006; Bröcker & Smith 2008; Laplace/KT/Jelinek-Mercer). Likewise, LLM-generated features into an interpretable bottleneck is 2023 work (Label-Free CBM; LaBo), and shuffle/random-feature/control-task substitutions are standard (Ojala & Garriga 2010; Stoppiglia et al. 2003; Kursa & Rudnicki 2010; Hewitt & Liang 2019).

What is genuinely absent from the literature is the specific inferential device: holding the fitted mixture weight fixed and swapping the added channel for an uninformative distribution, so that the reported quantity is the gain over a calibration-only null rather than the raw gain. That has no name in forecasting, ensembling, or ML evaluation. It is a real but small contribution, and it should be presented as a diagnostic protocol descended from control tasks, not as a new method.

Three concrete recommendations for the revision. First, the uniform floor is the WEAKEST available null — uniform is not the no-information distribution, the marginal choice distribution is. Report a ladder: (a) uniform at lambda-hat, (b) uniform with its own refit optimal weight, (c) marginal/climatological floor at its own optimal weight, (d) narratives shuffled within attribute strata, (e) narratives generated from observed attributes only. Nulls (c), (d) and (e) are the load-bearing ones; (d) and (e) are what actually answer 'perceived outcomes vs semantic expansion', and (c) is what actually answers 'is this calibration'. Second, stop reporting NLL as a scalar. Decompose it into reliability, resolution and uncertainty (Bröcker 2009; Weijs et al. 2010) and show the narrative channel moving the RESOLUTION term. A uniform floor can only move reliability, so a resolution gain is a measurement rather than an argument, and it disposes of reviewer concerns 2 and 3 at once. Also add a temperature-scaling-of-the-base-model-alone baseline (Guo et al. 2017): if that recovers most of the pooled gain, you need to know before the reviewers do. Third, the precedent that this kind of paper is publishable at a top venue is Abe et al., 'Deep Ensembles Work, But Are They Necessary?' (NeurIPS 2022) — an accepted paper whose contribution is a control showing a popular mechanism's gains have a mundane explanation. Frame the revision the same way: the method plus the protocol that makes its central claim falsifiable, with related work conceding the pooling machinery outright in one honest paragraph.
