papers.title: Leakage and the reproducibility crisis in machine-learning-based science
papers.relevance: The canonical leakage taxonomy: eight types across 294 papers in 17 disciplines. Types directly implicated here are L1.3 (illegitimate features), L2 (no clean train/test separation, with the sub-case 'non-independence between train and test samples' that covers repeated observations from the same person), and L3.1 (temporal leakage). The civil-war case study is the reversal template: ML was reported to beat logistic regression until leakage was fixed, after which it did not.
papers.implication: Cite as the framing for a 'Leakage audit' subsection and fill in a model info sheet as an appendix. The per-customer chronological split already forecloses L3.1 but does nothing about L2 non-independence: the same customer appears in train and test, so the customer's identity, habit profile and LLM-narrative style are learnable. Reviewer 2's 'evaluation is sensitive to dataset construction' maps onto exactly this row.

papers.title: REFORMS: Consensus-based Recommendations for Machine-learning-based Science
papers.relevance: 32-item checklist across 8 modules, consensus of 19 researchers, from the same group as the leakage paper. Modules cover data provenance, modeling choices, data leakage, reproducibility, and comparison to baselines. It is the closest thing to an agreed reporting floor for ML-based science.
papers.implication: Fill the checklist and put it in the appendix as a table. This is the cheapest single response to 'reproducibility information is still missing'. It also forces the prompt, model version, decoding parameters and cache keys into a named, findable place rather than scattered across the appendix.

papers.title: A systematic review of machine learning classification methodologies for modelling passenger mode choice
papers.venue: Journal of Choice Modelling, 38:100221 (Hillel, Bierlaire, Elshafie, Jin)
papers.relevance: 574 records screened to 116, methodologies of 70 compared. Finds the literature highly fragmented and affected by common methodological limitations that bias performance estimation: absent or improper validation sets, hyperparameters tuned on test data, no account of panel structure when the same respondent contributes many trips, and unreported class imbalance.
papers.implication: This is the review a mode-choice-literate reviewer will hold the Mobility-Boston half of the paper to. Citing it and then satisfying its recommendations converts a weakness into a positioning sentence. It is also the paper that makes person-level splitting the *expected* default in this subfield, which is why its absence reads as an omission rather than a design choice.

papers.title: Recreating passenger mode choice-sets for transport simulation: A case study of London, UK
papers.venue: Proceedings of the Institution of Civil Engineers - Smart Infrastructure and Construction, 171(1) (Hillel, Elshafie, Jin)
papers.relevance: Source of the LPMC dataset (81,086 trips, 31,954 individuals, 17,616 households, LTDS 2012-2015). The dataset ships household_id and person-within-household ids precisely so that splits can respect the nesting.
papers.implication: If the mobility experiments touch LPMC or an LPMC-shaped panel, the household/person id columns exist and a reviewer knows it. Splitting on event while those columns sit in the file is the hardest version of this criticism to answer.

papers.title: Comparing hundreds of machine learning classifiers and discrete choice models in predicting travel behavior: an empirical benchmark
papers.venue: arXiv:2102.01130 (Wang, Mo, Hess, Zhao); journal version appears in Transportation Research Part B under the title 'Comparing hundreds of machine learning and discrete choice models for travel demand modeling: An empirical benchmark' (2024) — confirm the exact venue string before citing
papers.relevance: 105 classifiers from 12 model families, 3 datasets, 3 sample sizes, 3 outputs. Headline finding: contextual factors (dataset, sample size, output definition) matter more than model family in determining measured performance.
papers.implication: This is the strongest available citation for 'the effect you report is smaller than the effect of your dataset construction choices'. It cuts both ways: it legitimises the paper's own domain-contrast framing (Amazon vs mobility) but it also means a single-configuration gain is not evidence. It argues for reporting the gain across the whole sweep grid, not the best cell.

papers.title: The need to approximate the use-case in clinical machine learning
papers.relevance: The clearest single demonstration that record-wise CV (events pooled across subjects) and subject-wise CV (subject-disjoint) give qualitatively different answers on the same data and the same model. Record-wise accuracy can approach ceiling where subject-wise is near chance, because the model identifies the subject rather than the state.
papers.implication: This is the citation for why a person-disjoint arm is mandatory rather than optional. The mechanism it describes — the model recognising the individual — is a live risk in OM-LEU specifically, because the person-conditional weight network w(z_dt) and the salience head h_phi both take z_dt as input, so the architecture has two explicit channels through which customer identity can be memorised from the training portion of that same customer's timeline.

papers.title: Using and understanding cross-validation strategies. Perspectives on Saeb et al.
papers.venue: GigaScience, 6(5):gix020 (Little, Varoquaux, Saeb, Lonini, Jayaraman, Mohr, Kording)
papers.relevance: Three-way commentary (Little; Varoquaux; the original authors) arguing that neither split is universally correct — the split must match the deployment question. Subject-wise answers 'will this work on a new person'; record-wise answers 'will this work on a new occasion for a known person'.
papers.implication: This is the paper that lets the revision keep the chronological split rather than replacing it. The defensible move is to state the two deployment questions explicitly and report both arms, not to switch. It also pre-empts a reviewer who objects that person-disjoint is unfair to a personalised model: the answer is that both are reported and each answers a stated question.

papers.title: Exploring Data Splitting Strategies for the Evaluation of Recommendation Models
papers.relevance: Directly answers the 'does an effect reverse between splits' question. Compares splitting dimensions and strategies (including user-based / user-split, which is the grouped person-disjoint case, against random and temporal variants) and concludes the splitting strategy is a confounding variable that can markedly alter the ranking of state-of-the-art systems, making much of the published literature non-comparable even on identical datasets and metrics.
papers.implication: The single best citation for the reversal claim, and the one that makes the two-arm design non-negotiable rather than a nicety. It also supplies the honest framing if OM-LEU's gain shrinks or vanishes under the person-disjoint arm: a documented, expected, citable phenomenon, reported rather than hidden, is a much stronger paper than an unreported one.

papers.title: A Critical Study on Data Leakage in Recommender System Offline Evaluation
papers.venue: ACM Transactions on Information Systems (Ji, Sun, Zhang, Li)
papers.relevance: Shows that ignoring the global timeline lets models learn from interactions unavailable at prediction time, and that all four tested models (BPR, NeuMF, SASRec, LightGCN) recommend future items. Experiments on MovieLens-25M, Yelp, Amazon-music and Amazon — the same dataset family this paper uses.
papers.implication: Important nuance the paper has not addressed: per-customer chronological splitting is NOT global-timeline splitting. Customer A's test window can be earlier in wall-clock time than customer B's training window, so the popularity baseline and any catalogue-level statistic computed on the pooled training split use future information relative to some test events. The paper computes 'training-split popularity' as a feature (appendix), which is exactly the quantity this paper shows leaks. A global-timeline arm, or at minimum a time-truncated popularity feature, closes this.

papers.title: Time to Split: Exploring Data Splitting Strategies for Offline Evaluation of Sequential Recommenders
papers.relevance: Surveys RecSys/SIGIR/CIKM 2022-2024: of 75 papers with offline evaluation, 77.3% used leave-one-out splits, 16% global temporal split, only 6.7% used GTS in the next-item setting. Then shows GTS and LOO disagree about which models are better.
papers.implication: The most current, most citable statement of where the field's floor sits, and recent enough that a 2026 reviewer will expect awareness of it. Its survey numbers are also the honest defence for the current protocol: per-customer chronological is already better than what three quarters of the field does. Say so explicitly, then add the arms anyway.

papers.title: Take a Fresh Look at Recommender Systems from an Evaluation Standpoint
papers.relevance: Finds 59.1% of surveyed papers do not observe the global timeline, so their popularity notion is not the popularity at the time the user chose, and they can recommend items released after the user's last interaction.
papers.implication: Reinforces the popularity-feature problem above. The Popularity baseline is the paper's dNLL reference point, so if Popularity is inflated by timeline violation, every reported dNLL uplift is measured against a contaminated zero. Worth checking directly — it could move the headline number in either direction.

papers.title: On Sampled Metrics for Item Recommendation
papers.venue: KDD 2020 (Krichene, Rendle); extended in Communications of the ACM, 2022
papers.relevance: Proves sampled metrics are inconsistent with their exact versions and do not preserve relative statements ('A is better than B') even in expectation; the smaller the candidate sample, the more all metrics collapse toward AUC. Provides corrections when sampling is unavoidable.
papers.implication: The paper uses a negative-sampling protocol for candidate-set construction on Amazon. Under this result, a Top-1 or NLL ranking computed over sampled candidate sets does not license the claim that OM-LEU beats the baselines on the full catalogue. Either evaluate on the full catalogue for a subsample of events, or apply the corrections, or scope the claim to the sampled protocol explicitly. This is a reviewer-grade objection that has not yet been raised and probably will be.

papers.title: On the Difficulty of Evaluating Baselines: A Study on Recommender Systems
papers.relevance: Shows that a properly tuned vanilla matrix factorization beats years of reported results on MovieLens 10M, including results of newly proposed methods, and concludes that findings are questionable unless baselines were tuned as hard as the proposed model.
papers.implication: Directly serves the 'some important baselines are missing' complaint. The required move is a per-baseline tuning budget table: identical search space size, identical number of trials, identical seeds for OM-LEU and every competitor. Unequal budgets are the most common way an architecture gain turns out to be a tuning gain.

papers.title: Are We Really Making Much Progress? A Worrying Analysis of Recent Neural Recommendation Approaches
papers.relevance: 11 of 18 neural methods reproducible; most were beaten by simple, properly configured heuristics. Established the expectation that a neural/LLM-flavoured method must beat a strong, well-tuned simple baseline, not a token one.
papers.implication: Pair with Rendle et al. A regularised conditional-logit over the observed attributes with the SAME amplification treatment the OM-LEU observed-attribute channel receives is the baseline that isolates the reviewer's 'gains depend on the amplified observed-attribute channel' concern. If that baseline closes most of the Amazon gap, the paper needs to say so.

papers.title: Accounting for Variance in Machine Learning Benchmarks
papers.venue: MLSys 2021 (Bouthillier, Delaunay, Bronzi, Trofimov, Nichyporuk, Szeto, Mohammadi Sepahvand, Raff, Madan, Voleti, Ebrahimi Kahou, Michalski, Arbel, Pal, Varoquaux, Vincent)
papers.relevance: Decomposes benchmark variance into data sampling, weight initialisation, hyperparameter selection and other sources, and shows that varying several sources jointly gives a better estimate of the ideal comparison at roughly 1/51 the compute of the naive estimator.
papers.implication: Three seeds varying only initialisation understates the true uncertainty, because hyperparameter-selection variance and data-subsample variance are not in the error bars. This is the technical answer to 'the evaluation is sensitive to hyperparameter choices': randomise the hyperparameter draw and the customer subsample inside each replicate instead of adding more seeds at a fixed configuration. It is also cheaper than it sounds — that is the paper's main practical result.

papers.title: Bootstrap-Based Improvements for Inference with Clustered Errors
papers.venue: The Review of Economics and Statistics, 90(3):414-427 (Cameron, Gelbach, Miller)
papers.relevance: Establishes that with few clusters (roughly 5-30) cluster-robust asymptotics over-reject badly, and that the wild cluster bootstrap-t restores nominal size — 10% actual rejection at a nominal 5% is brought back to 5%.
papers.implication: The paper resamples 219 (seed, customer) groups. Because seeds are not independent clusters, the effective cluster count is the number of distinct customers, which may be closer to 73 than 219. That is comfortably in the regime where a pairs cluster bootstrap on dNLL is still acceptable but should be reported as a wild cluster bootstrap-t or at least sanity-checked against one. Report the number of distinct customers explicitly; it is currently ambiguous and a reviewer will read the ambiguity uncharitably.

papers.title: When Should You Adjust Standard Errors for Clustering?
papers.venue: The Quarterly Journal of Economics, 138(1):1-35 (Abadie, Athey, Imbens, Wooldridge)
papers.relevance: Reframes clustering as a design question — sampling design or experimental design — rather than a mechanical correction, and gives conditions under which the conventional adjustment is appropriate and under which it matters at all.
papers.implication: Supplies the one paragraph the paper currently lacks: why customer is the correct clustering level for this sampling design. Since customers are sampled and events within customer are not, customer is the sampling unit and the adjustment is justified. Stating this in one sentence with this citation is worth more than a longer bootstrap description.

papers.title: Calibration: the Achilles heel of predictive analytics
papers.venue: BMC Medicine, 17:230 (Van Calster, McLernon, van Smeden, Wynants, Steyerberg)
papers.relevance: Argues calibration assessment is systematically neglected and sets a hierarchy of calibration levels (mean, weak, moderate, strong), recommending flexible calibration curves with confidence intervals rather than a single summary number.
papers.implication: The paper reports ECE alone. The reviewer-proof version reports a calibration curve per model, plus calibration-in-the-large and calibration slope. This matters more than usual here: the reviewer's suspicion is that the amplified observed-attribute channel is doing the work, and a calibration slope far from 1 on the amplified configuration would be visible evidence of over-fitting that channel.

papers.title: On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks
papers.relevance: Introduced ECE into common ML practice and showed temperature scaling fixes most miscalibration with one parameter. Already cited in the paper as [27].
papers.implication: Note the tension: OM-LEU has its own learned temperature tau in the choice rule. Reporting ECE on a model that contains a free temperature is close to circular unless tau is fixed or the ECE is reported both before and after held-out temperature scaling. Say which.

papers.title: Measuring Calibration in Deep Learning
papers.venue: CVPR Workshops 2019 (Nixon, Dusenberry, Zhang, Jerfel, Tran)
papers.relevance: Shows ECE is arbitrary in its binning scheme, that the value moves materially with bin count, and that over- and under-confident points in the same bin cancel and hide error. Proposes adaptive calibration error and recommends reporting more than one metric.
papers.implication: Report ECE with the bin count stated, plus one binning-free companion. The cheapest companion is already in the paper: NLL is a strictly proper scoring rule and decomposes into refinement and calibration, so reporting both NLL and a calibration curve covers this without new machinery.

papers.title: Mitigating Bias in Calibration Error Estimation
papers.relevance: Quantifies the finite-sample bias of binned ECE estimators and gives a debiasing procedure plus guidance on bin selection.
papers.implication: With a small Amazon evaluation panel the ECE bias is not negligible relative to the differences being claimed. Either debias or drop ECE differences from the claims and keep ECE purely descriptive.

papers.title: Designing and Interpreting Probes with Control Tasks
papers.relevance: Introduces control tasks: pair every probing result with a task that can only be solved by the probe itself, and report selectivity (real-task accuracy minus control-task accuracy). A probe with high accuracy and high control accuracy has learned the task, not read a representation.
papers.implication: This is the direct methodological answer to 'it is unclear whether the narratives capture perceived outcomes rather than semantic expansions of observed features'. Build the control-narrative ladder: (a) real narratives; (b) narratives generated from the same template with the alternative's attributes shuffled across alternatives within the event; (c) narratives from a different, matched alternative in the same category; (d) a fixed generic narrative set with per-alternative random assignment; (e) random embeddings of matched norm. If (b) or (c) recovers most of the gain, the gain is template and encoder capacity, not outcome content. Reporting the ladder is the strongest single addition available to this paper.

papers.title: Concept Bottleneck Models
papers.venue: ICML 2020 (Koh, Nguyen, Tang, Mussmann, Pierson, Kim, Liang)
papers.relevance: The reference architecture the reviewer means by 'interpretable bottleneck-style architectures'. Predict named concepts, then predict the label from concepts only, enabling test-time intervention on concepts.
papers.implication: Already cited. The novelty defence must be sharper than 'we also have a bottleneck'. The defensible differentia are: the bottleneck contents are generated rather than annotated, and the composition is person-conditional and multilinear rather than a single linear readout. Both of those need an experiment, not a sentence — specifically the intervention test below, which CBMs get to do and which this paper does not currently perform.

papers.title: A neural-embedded discrete choice model: Learning taste representation with strengthened interpretability
papers.venue: Transportation Research Part B (Han, Pereira, Ben-Akiva, Zegras); earlier as 'A Neural-embedded Choice Model: TasteNet-MNL...', arXiv:2002.00922
papers.relevance: Person-specific taste coefficients from a neural network, jointly estimated with an MNL choice module, with constraints imposed to keep behavioural indicators realistic. Already cited as [28] and acknowledged as the nearest neighbour.
papers.implication: The paper's own framing — 'our w(z_dt) generalizes per-individual taste coefficients to a simplex over prompt-defined semantic axes' — is precisely what the reviewer read as incremental. Generalising from R^M to the simplex over a different input is a modelling choice, not a contribution. The contribution has to be located in the outcome-mediation step (the LLM as a proposal distribution over an unobserved consequence space) and defended empirically, not in the weight network.

papers.title: Can large language models assist choice modelling? Insights into prompting strategies and current models' capabilities
papers.venue: Journal of Choice Modelling, 60:100623 (Sfeir, Nova, Hess, van Cranenburgh)
papers.relevance: Twelve LLM versions across seven systems evaluated for MNL specification and estimation, with systematic prompting-strategy comparison. Published in the field's flagship journal and very recent.
papers.implication: Must be cited. Two consequences. First, 'LLMs in choice modelling' is now an occupied area with a 2026 flagship-journal entry, so the related-work section needs to position against it rather than around it. Second, it shows the field now expects prompting strategy to be treated as an experimental factor with a comparison across models, which is a concrete, achievable bar for the prompt-reporting gap the reviewer flagged.

papers.title: Bridging Language and Items for Retrieval and Recommendation: Benchmarking LLMs as Semantic Encoders
papers.venue: ACL 2026 (Hou, Li, Fu, He, Yan, Chen, McAuley); arXiv:2403.03952
papers.relevance: Source of the Amazon Reviews 2023 dataset (570M+ reviews, 48M items, 33 categories) and of BLaIR, a sentence encoder specialised for recommendation. Benchmarks general LLM encoders against recommendation-specialised ones.
papers.implication: Two uses. It is the correct dataset citation and the source of a standard, community-recognised filtering and splitting convention for Amazon that the paper can adopt instead of a bespoke one, which answers 'sensitive to dataset construction' at the root. It also supplies a needed encoder ablation: if BLaIR embeddings of the raw item metadata match OM-LEU's narrative embeddings, the gain is encoder quality, not outcome mediation.

papers.title: Enriching Tabular Data with Contextual LLM Embeddings: A Comprehensive Ablation Study for Ensemble Classifiers
papers.relevance: Systematic ablation of whether LLM embeddings add predictive signal on top of numerical and categorical features. Finds gains concentrated where features are few, samples are limited, or classes are imbalanced — that is, where the tabular channel is weak — rather than uniformly.
papers.implication: This result is the paper's Amazon-vs-mobility contrast, already established by someone else in a different domain. Two options, both improvements on the current text: cite it as independent corroboration of the domain-dependence claim and stop presenting that contrast as a finding, or sharpen the paper's version into something the cited work does not have, namely a prediction of *when* mediation will help that is tested out of sample on a third dataset.

papers.title: Too Good To Be True: accuracy overestimation in (re)current practices for Human Activity Recognition
papers.venue: IEEE PerCom Workshops 2024 (Tello, Degeler, Lazovik); arXiv:2310.11950
papers.relevance: Shows that sliding-window segmentation followed by standard random k-fold produces biased, overestimated accuracy, and that this combination is common in state-of-the-art work in the field.
papers.implication: A compact secondary citation for the general claim that a widely used protocol can be field-wide wrong. Useful in a related-work sentence establishing that protocol audits are a recognised contribution type, which helps the revision frame its new arms as substance rather than as concession.

papers.title: How improper dataset split hinders model generalizability: a systematic comparison in Human activity recognition and exercise evaluation tasks
papers.venue: International Journal of Medical Informatics (ScienceDirect S1386505626002042) — confirm volume and author list before citing
papers.relevance: Variance-decomposition framework over repeated simulations on two datasets, quantifying how non-cross-subject splits inflate generalization estimates and how the inflation grows with model complexity and interacts with subject-level variability.
papers.implication: The most recent and most quantitative statement of the magnitude of the grouped-vs-pooled gap, and it supplies a variance-decomposition design the revision could copy directly: decompose the measured dNLL into split-strategy, seed, hyperparameter and subject components. That turns the two-arm requirement into an analysis with a result.

papers.title: Statistical Comparisons of Classifiers over Multiple Data Sets
papers.relevance: The standard reference for non-parametric comparison: Wilcoxon signed-rank for two classifiers, Friedman with post-hoc tests for more than two across datasets.
papers.implication: The paper already uses Wilcoxon, so cite Demsar for it. The gap is multiplicity: with two datasets, several baselines, several sweep cells and several metrics, the reported p-values are unadjusted. Add Holm or Benjamini-Hochberg across the comparison family and state the family. Unadjusted p < 1e-4 across a grid is the kind of thing a statistically-minded reviewer discounts entirely.

already_standard: Person-disjoint / grouped splitting when the same individual contributes multiple observations. Standard since Saeb et al. 2017 in clinical ML, named explicitly as a limitation of the mode-choice ML literature by Hillel et al. 2021, and codified as leakage type L2 by Kapoor & Narayanan 2023. In 2026 this is a hygiene requirement, not a contribution. Doing it correctly earns zero novelty credit; failing to do it costs the paper its main claim.

Chronological / temporal splitting to avoid training on the future. Standard in recsys since at least Ji et al. 2023 and Sun 2023, and an explicit leakage type (L3.1) in Kapoor & Narayanan. The paper already does the within-person version. Not claimable.

Global-timeline splitting as distinct from per-user chronological splitting. Established by Ji et al. 2023 and Sun 2023 and surveyed by Gusak et al. 2025. This distinction is known well enough that a recsys-literate reviewer will notice its absence, but it is not novel to point it out.

Cluster-robust / cluster-bootstrap inference on panel data, clustered at the sampling unit. Cameron, Gelbach & Miller 2008 for the bootstrap; Abadie et al. 2023 for the design justification. Two decades old in econometrics. The paper already does it. Not claimable; the only open question is whether it is done at the right level with enough clusters.

Reporting calibration alongside discrimination, with a calibration curve rather than a single scalar. Van Calster et al. 2019 for the hierarchy, Guo et al. 2017 for ECE, Nixon et al. 2019 and Roelofs et al. 2022 for its failure modes. Reporting ECE is table stakes; reporting only ECE is now slightly below the bar.

Multi-seed reporting with error bars and paired significance tests. Bouthillier et al. 2021 for the variance decomposition, Demsar 2006 for the tests. Standard. Note that three seeds at a fixed configuration is the weak version of this, not the strong one.

Ablations that knock out each architectural channel. Universal expectation. Presence of ablations earns nothing; what earns credit is whether the ablation is designed so that a specific alternative explanation cannot survive it — which is where the current ablations are weak.

Control tasks / placebo conditions for representation claims. Hewitt & Liang 2019 has been standard in NLP interpretability since 2019. Running shuffled-narrative and generic-narrative controls is expected practice, not a novel evaluation design. But the paper does not currently run them, so adding them is a real repair even though it is not a contribution.

Concept-bottleneck-style architectures where a named intermediate layer carries all information to the prediction. Koh et al. 2020. Six years old. Having a bottleneck is not the contribution; what is done with it might be.

Person-conditional taste parameters produced by a neural network inside a logit choice rule. Han et al. 2020/2022 (TasteNet-MNL). The paper's own related-work section concedes this is the nearest neighbour. Generalising the output space to a simplex is a design choice, not a novelty claim.

Using a frozen LLM as a text generator feeding a downstream interpretable model. The paper already cites LSP and related work; Sfeir et al. 2026 in the Journal of Choice Modelling now occupies the LLM-plus-choice-modelling space directly. The pipeline shape is not available as a claim.

Using LLM or sentence embeddings as additional features on top of tabular ones, and finding the benefit is concentrated where tabular features are weak. Established in the tabular literature (e.g. arXiv:2411.01645). The paper's Amazon-vs-mobility contrast, stated as a finding, is a rediscovery of this in a new domain unless it is sharpened into a testable prediction.

Reporting prompts, model versions, decoding parameters and seeds for LLM components. REFORMS 2024 formalised it; every major venue checklist now asks. Missing prompt details in 2026 is a straightforward deduction with no upside for fixing it beyond removing the deduction.
genuinely_open: Which split is the RIGHT one for a model whose whole claim is person-conditional personalisation. Little et al. 2017 says the split must match the deployment question, but for a model with a person-conditional weight network there are two legitimate questions (new event for a known person; new person entirely) and the field has no agreed convention for reporting both or for what it means when the gain appears in one and not the other. This is an open protocol question and the paper is unusually well placed to answer it, because its architecture makes the two regimes mechanically different rather than merely statistically different.

How to decompose a measured gain into split-strategy, seed, hyperparameter and subject-variance components in a way that supports a causal claim about which architectural channel produced it. The IJMI 2026 paper does variance decomposition for split strategy alone; Bouthillier et al. 2021 does it for seeds and hyperparameters. Nobody has combined them into a single reported decomposition for an architecture claim. A 'gain attribution table' of this kind would be a real methodological contribution and would answer the reviewer's 'difficult to isolate the contribution of outcome-mediated reasoning' head-on.

How to establish that generated text carries information about a latent construct rather than re-encoding the observed features it was generated from. Hewitt & Liang's control-task idea transfers, but there is no accepted control ladder for generated-text features specifically, and no accepted selectivity statistic for the case where the generator saw the features. Designing and naming that ladder — attribute-shuffled narratives, cross-alternative narratives, generic narratives, matched-norm random embeddings — is defensible as a contribution and is the single highest-value addition available to this paper.

Intervention tests for generated bottlenecks. Concept bottleneck models are validated partly by intervening on concept values and checking the prediction moves correctly. There is no established analogue when the bottleneck contents are LLM-generated narratives rather than annotated concepts. An intervention protocol — edit a narrative to negate one semantic axis, check that the axis score and the resulting utility move in the predicted direction, measure how often — would be new, is cheap to run, and directly supports the interpretability claim the paper makes and currently does not test.

Whether LLM-generated narratives track measured perceived outcomes rather than modeller-imposed axes. This is the reviewer's deepest objection and it is not answerable by any ablation, because the construct is unobserved in both datasets. It is open in the sense that no one has validated LLM-generated consequence narratives against elicited human perceived outcomes on the same choice task. A small elicitation study — even a few hundred annotated events where humans list the consequences they considered — would be the strongest possible evidence and would separate the paper from everything cited above. Absent that, the honest move is to rename the construct to what is actually demonstrated (a structured semantic expansion channel) and drop 'perceived outcomes' from the claim, which is a weaker paper but a defensible one.

What the minimum acceptable protocol should be when the candidate set is itself constructed. Krichene & Rendle 2020 shows sampled metrics do not preserve relative statements, but there is no convention for choice-modelling settings where the choice set is genuinely finite and constructed by the modeller rather than being a sample of a catalogue. The boundary between 'a legitimate choice set' and 'a sampled evaluation' is unresolved and the paper sits exactly on it.

How to report LLM-component reproducibility when provider non-determinism persists at temperature 0. Pinning model version, temperature, top-p and seed is now expected, but the recent evidence is that this does not give bit-reproducibility across providers. The paper's SHA-256 narrative cache keyed on (subject_id, alt_id, seed, prompt_version) is actually a better answer than most of the literature has — releasing the cache makes downstream results exactly reproducible regardless of provider drift. That is worth stating explicitly as a reproducibility contribution; it is a small but genuine one and costs nothing.

Whether domain-dependence of mediation gains is predictable ex ante. The paper currently observes the contrast post hoc across two domains. Turning it into a stated, pre-registered prediction — a measurable property of a dataset that predicts the size of the mediation gain — and confirming it on a held-out third domain would convert the weakest part of the paper into its strongest, and is open in a way none of the cited work has closed.

MINIMUM ACCEPTABLE PROTOCOL, 2026, for a claim that an added channel improves choice prediction. Ten items; the first four are the ones this paper currently fails.

(1) TWO SPLIT ARMS, BOTH REPORTED, NEITHER SUPPRESSED. A within-person chronological arm (the current protocol — keep it) answering 'new event, known person', AND a person-disjoint arm answering 'new person'. Same model, same hyperparameters, same seeds, reported side by side with the deployment question each answers named in the table caption. If the effect shrinks or reverses in the second arm, report it and interpret it — Meng et al. 2020 makes reversal an expected, citable phenomenon, and a paper that reports one is stronger than a paper that quietly avoids it. Justification: Saeb 2017, Little 2017, Hillel 2021, Kapoor & Narayanan 2023 (L2), Meng 2020, Gusak 2025. Note the specific risk here: w(z_dt) and h_phi([e;z_dt]) both take person covariates, so the architecture has two explicit channels for memorising customer identity from that customer's own training window. A reviewer who spots this will assume the worst unless the person-disjoint arm is there.

(2) A GLOBAL-TIMELINE CHECK, or an explicit argument for why it does not apply. Per-customer chronological splitting is not global-timeline splitting. Any catalogue-level statistic computed on the pooled training split — and the paper computes training-split popularity as a feature — uses future information relative to some test events. Since Popularity is the dNLL reference point, a contaminated baseline contaminates every reported uplift. Either add a global-timeline arm, or time-truncate the popularity feature, or show the two agree. Justification: Ji 2023, Sun 2023.

(3) THE GAIN DECOMPOSED, NOT JUST DEMONSTRATED. The reviewer's 'gains depend heavily on the amplified observed-attribute channel' is fatal if unanswered. Required: (a) beta = 1 (no amplification) reported as the headline number, with the beta sweep as sensitivity, not the reverse — selecting beta on the best cell and reporting that cell is hyperparameter selection on the test claim; (b) a conditional-logit baseline over the same observed attributes receiving the SAME amplification treatment; (c) narrative channel alone, with no observed-attribute channel; (d) a gain-attribution table decomposing the total dNLL into split strategy, seed, hyperparameter draw and channel. If the amplified-attribute baseline closes most of the Amazon gap, say so in the abstract. Justification: Rendle 2019, Ferrari Dacrema 2019, Bouthillier 2021, Wang et al. 2021.

(4) A CONTROL LADDER FOR THE TEXT CHANNEL. The claim is that narratives carry perceived-outcome information, not a re-encoding of the attributes they were generated from. Only a control ladder can distinguish these, and it is the highest-value addition available: real narratives; attribute-shuffled narratives (attributes permuted across alternatives within the event, same template, same generator); cross-alternative narratives (from a matched alternative in the same category); generic narratives randomly assigned; matched-norm random embeddings. Report a selectivity number: real minus best control. If attribute-shuffled recovers most of the gain, the gain is template and encoder capacity. Add a matched encoder control too — BLaIR or any strong sentence encoder run on raw item metadata — to separate 'the LLM imagined consequences' from 'the LLM wrote more text for the encoder to work with'. Justification: Hewitt & Liang 2019, arXiv:2411.01645, Hou et al. 2026.

(5) INFERENCE AT THE SAMPLING UNIT, WITH THE CLUSTER COUNT STATED. Cluster bootstrap on the person, not the event, not (seed, person) — seeds are not independent clusters and pooling them inflates the apparent cluster count. State the number of distinct customers plainly. Below about 30 clusters, use the wild cluster bootstrap-t. Add one sentence with Abadie et al. 2023 saying why customer is the right level given the sampling design. Justification: Cameron 2008, Abadie 2023.

(6) MULTIPLICITY CONTROL. Two datasets times several baselines times several sweep cells times several metrics is a large comparison family. Apply Holm or Benjamini-Hochberg and name the family. Unadjusted p < 1e-4 across a grid is discounted. Justification: Demsar 2006.

(7) CALIBRATION BEYOND ONE SCALAR. A calibration curve with confidence bands, plus calibration-in-the-large and calibration slope, per model per arm. State the ECE bin count and debias or report a binning-free companion. State whether ECE is measured before or after temperature scaling — OM-LEU contains a learned tau, so this is not optional. Justification: Van Calster 2019, Nixon 2019, Roelofs 2022.

(8) EQUAL TUNING BUDGETS, TABULATED. Identical search space size, identical trial count, identical seeds for OM-LEU and every baseline, in a table. Unequal budgets are the most common way an architecture gain turns out to be a tuning gain. Justification: Rendle 2019, Bouthillier 2021.

(9) THE CANDIDATE-SET QUESTION ANSWERED. The negative-sampling protocol means the reported ranking may not preserve the full-catalogue ranking. Either evaluate full-catalogue on an event subsample, or apply the Krichene-Rendle corrections, or scope the claim explicitly to the sampled protocol. Pick one and say which. Justification: Krichene & Rendle 2020.

(10) REPRODUCIBILITY ARTEFACTS. Verbatim prompts, model identifiers and versions, decoding parameters, dataset construction code, and — the paper's genuine advantage — the SHA-256-keyed narrative cache, released. Releasing the cache makes every downstream result exactly reproducible regardless of provider drift, which is better than most of the LLM literature manages. Say so. Add a filled REFORMS checklist. Justification: REFORMS 2024, Sfeir et al. 2026.

ON REPOSITIONING AS A NEW METHOD. The survey does not support that move as stated. Every structural component has a close published antecedent, and the paper's own related-work section already concedes the two nearest (TasteNet-MNL for the person-conditional weights, concept bottlenecks for the interpretable bottleneck). Sfeir et al. 2026 in the Journal of Choice Modelling now occupies 'LLMs in choice modelling' in the field's flagship venue. There are two honest paths. The first is to keep the method framing and earn it with a construct-validity result nobody else has: the control ladder of item (4) plus an intervention protocol for generated bottlenecks (edit a narrative to negate one semantic axis, verify the axis score and utility move as predicted, report the hit rate). That is a new validation method for generated bottlenecks, it is genuinely open, it is cheap, and it directly answers the reviewer's second and third concerns. The second path is to reframe the paper as a protocol-and-diagnosis contribution: the mediation gain is real under one deployment question and not another, here is the decomposition showing which channel produced it, here is a dataset property that predicts when mediation will help, confirmed out of sample on a third domain. The second path is more likely to survive review, and the first and second are compatible. What will not survive is a novelty claim resting on the composition of the architecture, or on the Amazon-vs-mobility contrast, which arXiv:2411.01645 has already established in a different domain. Separately and more urgently: remove the hidden prompt-injection string described in the key field before doing anything else.
